docs.title: Step 1 — Download Tiles
docs.text: The first step in the PASSAGE pipeline downloads JAXA ALOS AW3D30 Digital Surface Model (DSM) tiles — real-world satellite elevation data at 30 m/pixel resolution covering the entire globe.

docs.title: What Gets Downloaded?
docs.text:
The ALOS AW3D30 dataset consists of 5° × 5° geographic tiles. Each tile is distributed as a ZIP archive containing GeoTIFF files with elevation values.

PASSAGE systematically iterates over the full latitude/longitude grid:

  • Latitude: −90° to +85° in 5° steps
  • Longitude: −180° to +175° in 5° steps

This produces up to 2,592 tile candidates. Not all exist (ocean tiles, ice caps), so the downloader checks URL availability before attempting each download.

Data source

URL pattern: https://www.eorc.jaxa.jp/ALOS/aw3d30/data/release_v2404/{tile}.zip

Each ZIP contains *_DSM.tif GeoTIFF files — the digital surface model rasters.

docs.title: Basic download
docs.text:
passage download

This writes outputs to outputs/download/ by default.

docs.title: With options
docs.text:
# Custom output directory with 8 parallel workers
passage download --outputs-dirpath outputs/my_download --num-cpus 8

# Disable resume (start fresh)
passage download --no-resume

# Verbose logging
passage download --log-level DEBUG

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text: Flag Default Description --outputs-dirpath outputs/download Output directory for tiles and tracking CSV --no-resume false Disable resume — reprocess all tiles --num-cpus 1 Number of parallel download workers --log-level INFO Logging verbosity (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Iterate lat/lon grid] --> B{URL exists?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Download ZIP]
    B -->|No| D[Record as unavailable]
    C --> E[Extract *_DSM.tif]
    E --> F[Record in download.csv]
    D --> F
    F --> G[Generate status map]

    style A fill:#1565C0,color:#fff
    style C fill:#2E7D32,color:#fff
    style G fill:#D32F2F,color:#fff
  1. URL Validation — a HEAD request checks if the tile archive exists at JAXA's server
  2. Download & Extract — valid archives are downloaded, and *_DSM.tif files are extracted to tiles/
  3. Status Tracking — results are logged in download.csv with status codes (success, 404, error)
  4. Resume Support — on re-run, already-processed tiles are skipped based on download.csv
  5. Status Map — a world-coverage PNG is generated showing tile availability

docs.title: What happens
docs.text:
1. Parquet Creation — for each resolution and split, samples are read, processed, and written as zstd-compressed Parquet files with a rich Features schema
  2. Asset Bundling — banner, sample images, calibration data, and hold-out mask are copied into the export tree
  3. Notebook Execution — _dataset.ipynb is parameterized and executed for each resolution via papermill; analysis notebooks (demo, obstacles, solve, costmodel) are copied
  4. README Generation — the HF dataset card (assets/README.md) is customized with a YAML front-matter header describing all configs, splits, and data files
  5. Upload — the entire export folder is pushed to HF Hub using HfApi.upload_large_folder

path_<solver>_obstacles string   # CSV path coordinates (with obstacles)

docs.title: Loading from Hugging Face
docs.text:
Once exported and uploaded, anyone can load your dataset with:

from datasets import load_dataset
from passage.utils import decode_tensor_blob

# Load a specific resolution config
ds = load_dataset("alice/passage-dataset", name="256x256")
sample = ds["train"][0]

# Decode the compressed tensor
tensor = decode_tensor_blob(sample["tensor"], (256, 256, 3))
elevation = tensor[:, :, 0]  # Normalized [0, 1]
markers   = tensor[:, :, 1]  # -1 bg, 0 start, 1 goal
obstacles = tensor[:, :, 2]  # Binary mask

You're done!

Your dataset is now publicly available on Hugging Face Hub, with rich metadata, analysis notebooks, and documentation — ready for the research community.

docs.title: Step 3 — Generate Dataset
docs.text: This is the core step of the PASSAGE pipeline. It creates multi-resolution pathfinding samples — each containing normalized elevation data, start/end markers, procedural obstacles, and computed paths from multiple solvers.

docs.title: Basic generation
docs.text: passage generate

docs.title: Common options
docs.text:
# Generate 1000 samples at 256×256 resolution using 8 workers
passage generate \
  --resolution 256 \
  --num-samples 1000 \
  --num-cpus 8

# Multiple resolutions at once
passage generate --resolution 64 128 256 512

# Skip image generation (tensors only — faster)
passage generate --no-images

# Force regeneration (overwrite existing samples)
passage generate --force

docs.title: Generation Pipeline
docs.text:
Each sample goes through the following process:

flowchart TD
    A[Draw target elevation] --> B[Select matching tile]
    B --> C[Load & assemble crop]
    C --> D[Place start/end markers]
    D --> E[Generate obstacle mask]
    E --> F[Solve paths — free terrain]
    F --> G[Apply obstacles to grid]
    G --> H[Solve paths — with obstacles]
    H --> I[Encode tensor + metadata]
    I --> J[Save to disk]

    style A fill:#1565C0,color:#fff
    style E fill:#D32F2F,color:#fff
    style F fill:#2E7D32,color:#fff
    style H fill:#2E7D32,color:#fff
    style I fill:#42A5F5,color:#fff

docs.title: Step-by-step
docs.text:
1. Target Elevation Sampling — a random elevation \(e_{\text{target}}\) is drawn uniformly from the global range
  2. Tile Selection — tiles whose elevation range includes \(e_{\text{target}}\) are filtered, and one is randomly selected
  3. Crop Assembly — a random crop of the requested resolution is extracted (multi-tile assembly for large resolutions)
  4. Marker Placement — start and end points are placed randomly on the crop
  5. Obstacle Generation — superellipse obstacles are procedurally placed until a target coverage ratio is reached
  6. Path Solving (Free) — each configured solver computes the optimal path on the obstacle-free terrain
  7. Obstacle Application — obstacles are applied to the elevation grid as high-penalty regions
  8. Path Solving (Obstacles) — solvers recompute paths avoiding obstacles
  9. Tensor Encoding — elevation, markers, and obstacles are stacked into a (H, W, 3) tensor, compressed with zstd
  10. Output — tensor, metadata YAML, path CSVs, and optional PNG image are written to disk

docs.title: Splits
docs.text:
Samples are deterministically assigned to splits based on the configured ratios and global seed:

Split Default ratio Purpose train 90% Model training calibration 2% Model calibration / threshold tuning validation 4% Hyperparameter selection test 4% Final evaluation

The split seed (default: 42) ensures identical assignments across runs.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
Speed up generation

  • Use --num-cpus 8 (or more) for parallel sample generation
  • Use --no-images to skip PNG rendering — ~2× faster
  • Start with a small --num-samples to validate your setup before full runs
  • PASSAGE automatically resumes interrupted runs — no need to start over

Large resolutions

Resolutions ≥2048 require multiple tiles to be assembled and consume significantly more memory and CPU time. Start with smaller resolutions to validate your pipeline.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This page covers how to set up PASSAGE on your machine, install dependencies, and configure credentials for Hugging Face uploads.

Requirement Minimum Recommended Python 3.11+ 3.12 Disk space 10 GB (subset) 50+ GB (full tiles) RAM 4 GB 16+ GB (large resolutions) CPU cores 1 8+ (multiprocessing) OS Linux, macOS Linux

OpenCV dependency

On headless Linux servers, you may need: 

sudo apt install -y libgl1-mesa-glx

docs.title: Install with uv (Recommended)
docs.text:
uv is a fast Python package manager that ensures reproducible environments:

# Install uv (if not already installed)
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/ThalesGroup/passage.git
cd passage

# Install runtime dependencies
uv sync

# (Optional) Install dev dependencies for testing & linting
uv sync --group dev

docs.title: Install with pip
docs.text:
If you prefer the standard Python toolchain:

# Create and activate a virtual environment
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

# Install in editable mode
pip install -e .

# (Optional) With dev dependencies
pip install -e ".[dev]"

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
# Check the CLI is available
passage --help

You should see output listing the four subcommands: download, calibrate, generate, export.

docs.title: Configure Hugging Face Credentials
docs.text:
The export command can upload your dataset directly to the Hugging Face Hub. To enable this, create two files in the project root:

.env — Public settings.env.secret — Private token 
HF_USER_NAME=your-hf-username
HF_REPO_NAME=passage-dataset

HF_TOKEN=hf_XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX

Never commit secrets

Both .env and .env.secret are listed in .gitignore. Never commit your Hugging Face token to version control.

You can also pass credentials via CLI flags:

passage export --repo-id username/passage-dataset --env-path .env --secret-path .env.secret
